subtitle: Most trading journals are useless because they record the wrong things. The journal that improves your trading captures SETUP + REASONING + OUTCOME + LESSON. The journal that does NOT is one that just lists entries, exits, and PnL.

blocks.content:
You've been trading. You've taken winners and losers. The trades that lost — do you remember WHY they lost, beyond 'it didn't work'? The trades that won — do you remember which factor made them work? If not, you're operating with incomplete data on your own performance.

A trade journal is the system that builds this self-knowledge over time. But most retail journals are useless because they record the wrong things. The journal that improves you captures SETUP + REASONING + OUTCOME + LESSON. Each trade becomes a data point that compounds your knowledge.

rows: Discipline verification — was sizing within rules?
Categorization for pattern analysis (e.g., 'breakout retest', 'reversal at support', 'Wyckoff spring')
Which signals aligned (HTF support + RSI divergence + volume + ...)
Result, expressed in R (multiples of risk) not just dollar amount
Post-trade analysis — what played out vs your thesis
One specific takeaway from this trade

blocks.title: Useless fields to skip
blocks.content:
Don't pollute your journal with these:

  • Emotional rants: 'I feel like the market is rigged' — adds zero information, just vents.
  • Predictions about future market direction: 'I think BTC will go to $80K' — irrelevant to executed trades.
  • Detailed price tick-by-tick descriptions: 'Price moved from $60,123 to $60,145 then back to $60,128...' — noise, not signal.
  • Justifications for breaking rules: 'I sized up because I was sure' — recording this teaches you nothing useful.
  • Random unrelated thoughts: keep them in a personal journal, not the trading one.

The trading journal is for data that helps you trade better. Anything else clutters it and makes review harder.
The 'why' is the most important field

Most trade journals record what happened. The valuable ones record WHY YOU TOOK THE TRADE.

Examples:

  • Bad: 'Bought BTC at $60K, sold at $62K, +3%'
  • Good: 'Long BTC at $60K — 4H pullback to 50 EMA support + bullish engulfing + 2× volume + macro risk-on. SL $58.5K, TP1 $62K. Exited at $62K +3% as planned.'

The good entry lets you:

  • Recognize the same setup again next time.
  • Diagnose what worked when reviewing later.
  • Distinguish setup types and track their performance separately.

Track outcomes in R-multiples (multiples of risk), not just dollar amounts. Why:

  • R-multiples are comparable across trades regardless of size (a +2R trade on $10K notional is the same achievement as +2R on $100K).
  • R-multiples are comparable across accounts (your performance can be measured even as account grows).
  • R-multiples directly inform expectancy math: average R per trade × number of trades = total return.

Example: SL was 2% from entry, exited at 4% above entry = +2R (made 2× your risk). This metric is much more meaningful than '+$200 profit' which depends on size.
The lesson field — one specific takeaway

For each trade, write ONE specific lesson. Not 'I should trade better' (useless). Specific lessons look like:

  • 'Bullish engulfing at HTF support + volume = reliable; this is now a confirmed pattern for me'
  • 'I exited at TP1 instead of running TP2 — I'm too aggressive on profit-taking; need to use OCO for partial exits'
  • 'I held past my SL because I 'felt' it would bounce. Lost 3R. Always exit at SL — no exceptions'
  • 'Position sized too small because I was uncertain. Trade worked. Next time: if Apgar score 8+, use full normal size'

Specific lessons compound. After 100 trades you have 100 lessons. After 500 trades you have a personalized rulebook built from your own data.

rows: Brief review of all today's trades. Update journal entries. Note overall day performance.
Patterns across the week. Which setups worked, which didn't. Average R-multiple.
Bigger trends. Are certain setup types consistently winning? Losing? Adjust criteria.
Strategy-level review. Is your overall approach evolving as it should? What's working long-term?

blocks.content:
Over time, journal reviews reveal patterns you couldn't see while trading:

  • Your best setup types: maybe Wyckoff springs work for you but order block trades don't. Useful information for focus.
  • Your worst times of day: maybe you lose money in the first hour after waking up. Useful for scheduling.
  • Your behavioral patterns: maybe you over-trade after losses. Useful for self-discipline rules.
  • Your symbol preferences: maybe BTC works for you but alts don't. Useful for asset selection.

Without the journal, these patterns stay invisible. With it, they become actionable. The journal is how you become objective about your own trading.

blocks.title: Take this with you
blocks.content:
Three rules:

  1. Record SETUP + WHY + OUTCOME + LESSON for every trade. Not just numbers.
  2. Use R-multiples, not just dollar amounts.
  3. Review on a schedule: daily, weekly, monthly. Patterns reveal themselves over time.

This trading journal app has structured fields for most of this. Use them. Future-you reading the journal in 6 months will thank present-you for being thorough now.
